3483f1c747f03772: SEPTEMBER 16 — Every September 16, Malaysians come together to celebrate Malaysia Day, the day that marks the formation of Malaysia in 1963. It is a day that reminds us of the journey shared by Malaya, Sabah and Sarawak, and of the diversity that continues to shape the country we call home.

We often express that pride through our food, culture, language, traditions and the achievements of fellow Malaysians. But perhaps patriotism can also be reflected in something much more ordinary: the choices we make when we spend our money.
Does being Malaysian influence what we buy?

Walk into a supermarket or browse an online marketplace and the choices can be endless. Malaysian products sit alongside brands from Korea, Japan, China, the United States and many other countries. Yet among these choices are also businesses built by Malaysians, employing Malaysians and creating products inspired by the place we call home.

For some consumers, that connection matters. Choosing a Malaysian product can feel like more than a transaction. It can be a small way of supporting local entrepreneurs, celebrating Malaysian creativity and keeping part of our economic activity within the country.

However, pride does not always decide what goes into the shopping basket. Consumers still look at price, quality, convenience and reviews. A Malaysian brand may have a meaningful story, but consumers will expect the product to deliver. They want to know that their money is well spent and that the experience will meet their expectations.
This is where patriotism meets consumer behaviour. National pride can create an emotional connection, but the purchasing decision is often shaped by several factors at once.
A new generation of Malaysian consumers

The way Malaysians discover and evaluate products has also changed. Social media and e-commerce have made the marketplace more open than ever. A consumer can discover a local brand on TikTok, read reviews, compare prices and place an order without leaving home.

Young Malaysians in particular are growing up with a global marketplace at their fingertips. They can appreciate local culture while following international trends, buying products from overseas and discovering new brands through global social media platforms.

This should not be seen as a loss of national identity. It is simply a reflection of how consumer behaviour has evolved. Being Malaysian and being a global consumer can exist at the same time. For local businesses, however, it means that being Malaysian is no longer enough to stand out.
Giving consumers a reason to choose local

The phrase “support local” carries meaning, but it cannot be the entire marketing strategy. Consumers may be proud to support Malaysian businesses, but they also want products that fit their needs and lifestyles.

This is where Malaysian brands have an opportunity to turn local identity into something meaningful. Our culture, food, creativity and everyday experiences can provide stories that international brands cannot easily replicate. When these elements are combined with good products and a positive customer experience, they can create a stronger connection with consumers.
The key is authenticity. Consumers can tell the difference between a brand that genuinely understands Malaysian consumers and one that simply adds a patriotic message during a national celebration.

A Malaysian brand should not need to rely on the Jalur Gemilang or a Malaysia Day promotion to remind consumers where it comes from. Its Malaysian identity can be reflected naturally in the way it develops products, communicates with customers and builds its brand.
Patriotism at the point of purchase

Perhaps supporting Malaysian businesses does not mean choosing local every single time. There will always be situations where price, availability, quality or personal preference leads consumers in another direction.
What matters is that Malaysian businesses are given a fair chance to compete and that consumers recognise the value created by businesses within their own country.

Patriotism is often expressed through grand moments, but it can also exist in small everyday actions. Choosing a Malaysian product, recommending a local business or giving a home-grown brand an opportunity can be one of those actions.
This Malaysia Day, as we celebrate the country we share, perhaps we can also look at the choices we make as consumers.

Supporting Malaysian businesses does not mean choosing local products at every opportunity. It means recognising the value of what Malaysian entrepreneurs create and giving them the opportunity to earn our trust through the products and experiences they offer.

In the end, patriotism may influence where we look, but it is the value we receive that determines what we choose. For Malaysian brands, that is both a challenge and an opportunity to turn the pride of being local into a meaningful connection with consumers.

* Dr Nurul Fardini Zakaria is a Senior Lecturer in Marketing at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), with expertise in consumer behaviour, digital marketing, sustainable consumption and consumer welfare.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
fce5c946628f0281: Let’s agree at the outset the world is a complicated place, and social scientists have exacting jobs when it comes to measuring civic phenomena with precision.  After all, even careful studies raise follow-up questions: How much do their findings apply in other settings? Do conclusions about politics in one country apply to other countries? If you’re studying voters in a lopsided election, will your findings apply to voters in a close election? Those questions are all a natural part of the research process. That’s where Naoki Egami comes in. Egami is an MIT political scientist whose specialty is the methodology of research. He carefully scrutinizes, for one thing, what social scientists call “external validity,” whether the results of particular studies apply more generally. “I always say political methodology is the field where you ask questions as a political scientist, but then you solve them like an applied statistician or an applied computer scientist,” Egami says. “You find out the underlying mathematical problems behind the empirical challenges people face, and solve them optimally.” As it happens, Egami’s interests range widely. Years ago, before the current artificial intelligence craze, he started studying what happens when AI tools are introduced into studies. How accurate are they? How can researchers account for AI tendencies? Focusing on these and other questions has helped Egami build a broad portfolio of research, win awards, and flourish in his career. All the while, he retains interest in basic questions about politics, as well as measuring things correctly.  “You need both perspectives,” Egami says. “If you only think about technical statistical theories, you might not work on interesting empirical problems sometimes. But if you only think about problems, you won’t really solve them optimally; you’ll solve them in an ad-hoc way. So, you really want to have both lenses.” Egami joined MIT’s Department of Political Science as an associate professor with tenure in 2025. He is also a faculty affiliate of the Statistics and Data Science Center at the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS). Workshopping his career Almost anyone who likes their job has experienced some good fortune in finding it. Egami’s case calls to mind those adages about luck being a mixture of preparation and opportunity.  Egami grew up in Tokyo and attended the University of Tokyo. He was good at math and physics, but he also liked political philosophy and was unsure how to combine his interests. One day, Egami attended a workshop about U.S. graduate school, which he thought was about MBA programs. Actually, it was about PhD programs, and included a political scientist talking about using math in the field, so Egami asked her a question.  “The miracle is: That workshop had 200 people in it, and after it was done, I was packing my stuff to go home, and the panelist, who was a PhD student, came down from the stage and found me,” Egami recalls. “She asked, ‘Are you the one who said you’re interested in political science in the U.S., and likes math?’”  She invited Egami to what he thought would be another career workshop, the following week. Once again, he was mistaken. “I showed up, and it was an academic seminar,” Egami continues. “There were only 20 people there. It was 19 professors, and me, a first-year undergrad.” Then a professor named Kosuke Imai, now at Harvard University, gave a talk about his own research on using statistics in the social sciences.  “I was super-excited and felt if I could do even 20 percent of that, it would be a dream,” Egami says. “I talked to Kosuke and said, ‘I want to do what you’re doing.’ He probably thought I was just a random person.” Egami, thus bolstered, started pursuing the goal of becoming a political scientist. He received his BA after spending a year as an exchange student at the University of Michigan, and applied to graduate schools in the U.S., landing at Princeton University — where Imai eventually became one of his advisors. Working with Imai, Rafaela Dancygier, Brandon Stewart, and others, Egami generated papers on methodological topics like external validity — and found substantial interest when he presented them.  “That was a case where the audience or market told me what I should really work on,” Egami says. After earning his PhD from Princeton in 2020, he joined the faculty at Columbia University, moving to MIT five years later.  Enjoying the spirit of MIT One of the hallmarks of Egami’s work is very close scrutiny of the factors that can influence the results found in empirical studies.  “In statistics, you talk about whether the people in the data are similar, meaning the population data,” Egami says. “But in political science, there are a lot of differences in context.”  Consider the question of how much political campaigns sway the minds of voters. Political scientists have sometimes received permission to conduct field experiments in active political campaigns. That’s a significant step toward generating robust results. And yet, not all campaign settings are the same. Politicians may let researchers in when they expect to triumph, and the dynamics in those races might differ from close races.  “It’s great to do field experiments, and that’s usually where people are allowed to do research,” Egami says. “It’s where politicians know they can win. But most of the time, we’re interested in the battlefield races, the politically competitive districts. And the logic and voter behaviors can be different in those cases.”  Egami’s job, on one level, is to spot such differences and make other researchers aware of them. Meanwhile, he has also developed a strong interest in scrutinizing the tools of machine learning, as applied to the social sciences. This predates the elevated interested in AI generated by ChatGPT, starting in late 2022. Some of Egami’s work explores how to systematically identify errors introduced by AI tools and then account for this issue when using AI in research. “In the past, social science data is something we carefully collect and take a long time to really validate before we analyze it,” Egami says. “But if the generation of data is changing. If people use AI to generate data at scale, it can have errors. So I was already thinking: You want to have statistical methods that take into account these errors, otherwise many of the analyses will not be able to be replicated. That’s how I started to work on a lot of things about AI.”  All of this has brought Egami recognition and honors in the field. Last year, he received the Emerging Scholar Award from the Society for Political Methodology. He has also been the recipient of best paper awards from the American Political Science Association’s sections for political methodology (in 2019 and 2025), experimental research (in 2024), and political networks (in 2022). Earning awards in three subfields of the discipline speaks to Egami’s scholarly versatility. In his view, though, the work he does in different areas is ultimately aligned.  “All these things are in parallel,” Egami says. “I’m trying to start a new research agenda every three to four years. That helps me learn new topics and be motivated.” Further motivation, he says, comes from being at MIT and liking the experience. “I already knew MIT was an amazing place I would enjoy,” Egami says. Even so, in his time at MIT, he says, he has gained even more appreciation for the “spirit of engineering,” in the sense of working systematically on solutions to ongoing problems, among other things. In any case, Egami has found the Institute to be a stimulating and congenial place to do his work.  “People are really nice at MIT,” says Egami, who has been teaching both undergraduate and graduate classes. He adds: “The Department of Political Science is really high-functioning, people are intensive in terms of their work, but it’s just genuinely nice people.”  And, yes, that’s one claim about the world Egami does not have to double-check.
cb8bbffd4cfcb324: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's government has asked Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air whether they could absorb AirAsia's domestic market share, said two people with knowledge of the matter, as part of what they described as scenario planning while authorities monitor the financial health of Southeast Asia's largest low-cost airline.
Discussions between the government and Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air have increased in recent weeks, the people said, amid growing concerns over financial pressures faced by AirAsia.
The airline has been hit by soaring jet fuel costs stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran that surged 66% in the second quarter from the prior quarter to an average of US$183 a barrel.

The talks, which involve the finance ministry and state-linked airport operator Malaysia Airports Holdings Berhad (MAHB), are part of broader scenario planning around AirAsia's financial strains, the people said.

Other options that have been discussed include the government providing some form of endorsement to bolster the airline's plan to raise fresh capital from external investors, though the exact nature of any potential support remains unclear, Reuters reported this month.
Reuters was unable to independently establish details about AirAsia's financial picture.

Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air told the government they would only take over AirAsia's operations on a large scale if they could also assume its aircraft leases, one of the people said, as absorbing its routes and passenger volumes without the aircraft would be far more difficult.

Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air have both expressed to the government their willingness to expand organically to absorb AirAsia's routes and passengers rather than acquire its whole business, the people said.

AirAsia has said it commands about 40% of Malaysia's overall aviation market and 60% of domestic flying, making its financial challenges a significant concern for the government, the people interviewed by Reuters said.
Farouk Kamal, deputy group CEO of AirAsia Group, said in a statement that the airline does not comment on operational or financial speculation or unannounced corporate arrangements.
"All material updates regarding our business and fleet strategy are disclosed transparently through official exchange filings and corporate announcements at the appropriate time," he told Reuters.

"We also wish to reiterate that AirAsia remains focused on maintaining business continuity and stable operations across all its markets and we continue to see strong underlying demand across our network. We are also working closely with our stakeholders to manage our financial and operational requirements."

MAHB said it regularly engaged with all airline partners as part of normal network and route development, including on "potential capacity and route opportunities where there are gaps in the market or unmet demand." MAHB declined to comment on AirAsia's financial outlook.
Malaysia's finance ministry, Batik Air and Malaysia Airlines declined to comment.
AirAsia seeks fresh capital

AirAsia, which had current liabilities of RM18.4 billion (US$4.51 billion) as of June 30, owes MAHB at least RM500 million, the people and two others said, for services including landing and parking fees.
The airport operator has already granted the carrier repayment extensions, two of them said. They all declined to be identified because the discussions were private.

MAHB declined to comment on specific queries from Reuters, saying it did not discuss commercial arrangements with airline partners as a matter of practice. AirAsia did not address queries on whether it owed money to MAHB but said it had a strong and constructive relationship with key partners, including MAHB Chief Airports Officer Bryan Thompson and his team.

AirAsia said this month it was advancing discussions with financial institutions, targeting up to US$1 billion from international debt markets plus RM700 million in local credit facilities, primarily to restructure its debt.
Two of the people with knowledge of the matter estimated the airline required at least US$3 billion of fresh capital to address its financial position.
In response, AirAsia said its financing targets were sufficient to meet its requirements. The airline had cash and bank balances of RM954 million as of June 30.
AirAsia reported a net loss of RM831 million for the second quarter ended June 30, hit by rising jet fuel costs and heavy foreign-exchange losses of RM331 million.
The carrier has been restructuring aggressively, cutting underperforming routes, returning 25 older ‌aircraft to ⁠lessors and renegotiating contracts with vendors to reduce costs.

Reuters reported this month that the finance ministry had hired ‌Alton Aviation Consultancy to assess AirAsia's funding needs as it weighs whether to provide support given the airline's role as a major employer ​and provider of affordable air connectivity across the region.
The finance ministry declined to comment, while Alton did not respond to a request for comment.
0aa249329813e9bb: SEOUL, Sept 16 — A Seoul court ordered Pyongyang today to pay roughly US$32.5 million for blowing up in 2020 an office in North Korea that was intended to foster better relations between the two Koreas.
The lawsuit over the destruction of the Inter-Korean Liaison Office marks the first time the South Korean government has sought damages directly from the North Korean state, media reports said.

Experts consider it unlikely Pyongyang would ever pay damages over the demolition of the building in the North Korean city of Kaesong, and the South said it would “review the necessary follow-up measures”.
The office building was constructed in the dormant Kaesong Industrial Complex, where South Korean companies once employed North Korean workers.

But Pyongyang blew up the building in June 2020 after days of rising tensions when activists in the South sent balloons carrying anti-Pyongyang leaflets across the border, with the North denouncing the office as “useless”.
“The court has ruled the North should pay the South Korean government 44.6 billion won in damages,” a spokeswoman of the the Seoul Central District Court told AFP.
The case was filed in 2023 under the government of then South Korean leader Yoon Suk Yeol, which took a hardline on North Korea before he was ousted following his disastrous martial law declaration.
The office opened in September 2018, days before then South Korean president Moon Jae-in travelled to Pyongyang for his third summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Around 20 officials from each side were stationed at the office in the following months until operations were suspended in January 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Inter-Korean relations reached a high point in 2018, when Moon and Kim held three summits. But ties deteriorated after a meeting between Kim and US President Donald Trump in Hanoi collapsed in February 2019.
“It is simply impossible for the North to accept the responsibility and pay the damages,” Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told AFP.
“The North’s position on the demolition is clear: it maintains that the move was justified and was taken in response to faults by the South,” he added.
Whether the North responds to the ruling will depend on whether, and how, the South Korean government reacts publicly, he said.

South Korea’s Unification Ministry said “the government hopes that inter-Korean dialogue will resume and that all issues between the two Koreas can be resolved through dialogue and cooperation.” — AFP
c7812711b13e4f24: HONG KONG, Sept 16 — Asian stocks struggled today as investors prepare for an expected interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve later in the day, though there was a little support from a dip in oil prices following their recent run-up.

With inflation still running well above the central bank’s target and the Middle East crisis keeping crude above US$100 a barrel, monetary policymakers are widely tipped to lift borrowing costs for the first time since 2023.

That has dealt a heavy blow to a rally in global equities that saw several markets hit record highs in the first half of the year, and there is growing speculation that officials could announce another lift before the end of the year.
Fed boss Kevin Warsh last month ramped up bets on an increase when he delivered what was considered a hawkish speech at a gathering of central bankers and economists at Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

Since then, data showing strong jobs creation and stubbornly high inflation have cemented expectations, with traders pricing a more than 90 percent chance board members choose to tighten monetary policy.

Expectations that inflation will run hot for an extended time helped push up 10-year US Treasury yields this week above five percent and to a level not seen since 2007 before the global financial crisis kicked in.
“For traders, the most interesting part of the statement will be the vote, specifically how many of the 12 members (if any) vote to leave interest rates unchanged,” wrote Matt Weller at FOREX.com.

“If there are three or more dissents, or if Chairman Warsh himself dissents (unlikely), then even an immediate interest rate hike may be seen as a potential one-off ‘insurance hike’, rather than necessarily the start of a new rate hiking cycle.
“Conversely, a unanimous decision to raise rates makes another interest rate hike this year more likely.”

After a sell-off on Wall Street and in Europe, Asian equities staggered between gains and losses Wednesday, with tech firms still coming to terms with a call among top AI leaders for a slowdown in development in the sector.
Tokyo, Shanghai, Sydney and Manila fell, while Hong Kong, Singapore, Wellington, Taipei and Jakarta fell.
Seoul was flat.
The Fed announcement is followed Friday by the Bank of Japan, which is also expected to hike owing to rising inflation as well as the need to maintain support for the yen.
The currency has picked up against the dollar this month—having hit a 40-year low in July—helped by a historic joint Japan-US intervention.
But observers say it could benefit in the future from Fed struggles to rein in prices.
“Currency markets are still pricing in a consensus that US inflation will ultimately return to two per cent,” said Invesco’s David Chao.
“It is very possible that US inflation instead settles closer to three per cent.
“In such an environment where the central bank is seen as less credible in reigning in inflation, investors may become less willing to hold US dollars simply because US interest rates are higher.”
The Bank of England is forecast to maintain its benchmark rate tomorrow as the UK economy struggles for growth.

A drop in oil prices Wednesday provided some optimism, though both main contracts remain well above US$100 a barrel as the US and Iran remain at loggerheads and Saudi Arabia keeps a key pipeline closed following attacks.
Also in view, is a planned summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, with reports that they could agree to some tariff reductions.

Bloomberg said the two sides were looking at reductions on some goods including US energy and agricultural products, suggesting they will extend a one-year truce agreed in 2025 following Trump’s global tariff blitz.
6cde60a11b342a41: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 16 — Malaysian rally legend Karamjit Singh has given Terbang, the new film inspired by his life, his seal of approval — calling it about 60 per cent true to his story and hoping audiences will take inspiration from his refusal to give up.

The film, which opens in cinemas nationwide tomorrow, held its gala premiere at TGV Suria KLCC on Monday following months of production, with filming taking place in locations including Sepang, Perlis and New Zealand.

Directed by Chiu Keng Guan, the filmmaker behind acclaimed Malaysian films The Journey and Ola Bola, Terbang chronicles Karamjit’s journey to becoming an international rally champion and putting Malaysia on the global motorsport map.
‘Until the end, we never gave up’
Karamjit, who attended the gala premiere, said the film was about 60 per cent accurate to events in his life.

Several scenes were drawn from real experiences, including moments involving his wife, misunderstandings with his rally teammates and an international tournament where some competitors suspected he was cheating because they believed the car he was driving must have been illegal.
While Terbang dramatises those events for the big screen, Karamjit said he was proud to see his story become a film.
“Personally, I feel very proud about the movie.
“It is a true story and not fiction, and the story is about me until I became world champion.
“It is also about the teamwork of the Malaysian team — the driver and co-driver, mechanics, and everyone.
“Of course, I feel very proud, and I hope everybody will go and watch it and get inspiration from the movie because we never gave up.
“Until the end, we never gave up.
“There were times when the car broke down, and we thought we wouldn’t win it, but we did, in our first attempt in the first year,” he said.
Enough stories for a series
Speaking to Malay Mail, Karamjit said his rally career contained enough material for several more chapters should another film ever get the green light.
“This is only about the world championship (Terbang).
“We can talk about the Asia Pacific Championship, the Malaysia Championship and how I started with my father’s car, so it can actually be like a series, if you ask me,” he said.
“There is a lot more to be said.”

Produced by Astro Shaw in collaboration with EJJ Films, Enotech Pictures and Aventure Space, with WooHoo Pictures serving as the production house, Terbang marks a rare Malaysian foray into the rally-racing genre.
The film stars Irfan Zaini as Ajeet, a character inspired by Karamjit, alongside Jack Tan, Zizan Razak, Namron, Diana Danielle, Qasrina Karim and Shweta Sekhon.
The story follows Ajeet, who leaves rally racing behind in pursuit of a quieter life with his wife, Lisa, played by Shweta.
Five years later, fate draws him back to the track.
Teaming up with Kitt, a talented but hot-headed young driver played by Tan, Ajeet must confront his inner turmoil, fierce competition and a lingering guilt he has never truly shaken.
With Lisa’s support, the leadership of Rahim (Namron) and the expertise of Imran (Zizan), Ajeet and his team come together for a shot at competing on the world stage.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The team behind ‘Terbang’ at the film’s gala premiere at TGV Suria KLCC. — Picture courtesy of Astro Shaw
‘Our Malaysian way’ of telling the story
Head of Astro Shaw Raja Jastina Raja Arshad described Terbang as a Malaysian film made for audiences around the world.
“This is the first local film of this kind of genre or production quality you have seen,” she said, adding that Malaysia had not previously produced a film centred on rally racing.
“We hope that audiences in Malaysia will support Terbang, as this will give us an opportunity to do more of this and be braver in introducing more genres to Malaysians.”
She also touched on the extensive research that went into bringing Terbang to life, with Hazwani Mahayuddin contributing to the screenplay alongside the Astro Shaw writing team.
Hazwani said some of the scenes and stunts in the film were not exaggerations but were drawn from research into real-life rally tournaments.
“We used our Malaysian way to tell our Malaysian stories,” Chiu added of the approach taken with Terbang.
He said the film was not made with the intention of competing with other racing movies.
Terbang opens in Malaysian cinemas on September 17 and will also be available in 4DX.
For Karamjit, the film’s message is ultimately a simple one.
“Never giving up, you must believe in yourself, and also the takeaway is that if you work as a team, you can achieve wonders,” he said.
503bd91cde8ad659: PETALING JAYA: The terms of the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63) must be fulfilled, rather than replaced with a new agreement or “new deal”, said Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) secretary-general Armizan Mohd Ali.

In a Malaysia Day message, Armizan said he wants the value and meaning of Malaysia Day to come with a broader understanding and acceptance of every episode and chapter in the history of the formation of the country.

Armizan, who is also the domestic trade and cost of living minister, pointed out that the MA63 affirms the commitment and responsibility of all parties that agreed to sign the agreement to form the Federation of Malaysia.

He said Article VIII of MA63 required the governments of Malaya, North Borneo and Sarawak to take the necessary legislative, executive or other measures to implement the assurances, undertakings and recommendations under the Inter-Governmental Committee Report that are not already provided for in the Federal Constitution.

“Moving forward, the country does not need a new agreement or what some quarters have described as a ‘new deal’. This is because the terms of the agreement expressly demonstrate that MA63 did not cease to have effect once the Federal Constitution was enacted.
“Instead, MA63 remains a living document, with the commitments and responsibilities outlined in it remaining relevant and binding - past, present and forever,” he said in a statement.

The Papar MP said awareness of the nation’s history of independence requires not only an understanding of the Federation of Malaya Agreement 1948, the social contract among the three major communities, and Malaya’s independence in 1957.
“It also requires full acceptance of the birth certificate of the Federation of Malaysia itself - the MA63,” he said.
916376ebc6ecc26f: PETALING JAYA: DAP menggesa Jabatan Peguam Negara (AGC) segera mengatur taklimat rasmi bersama keluarga remaja yang maut ditikam di sebuah sekolah di Bandar Utama, susulan pembebasan remaja lelaki berusia 15 tahun yang didakwa membunuhnya.

e6f2fe221b89abe5: WASHINGTON: Health authorities in the eastern US state of Pennsylvania have confirmed a fourth death linked to measles, as the nation faces the largest outbreak of the vaccine-preventable disease in decades.
All four deaths occurred in unvaccinated individuals, state health officials said.

"My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades," said state health secretary Debra Bogen.
The latest death was of an 18-year-old, according to local medical examiners, adding to two infants who were too young to be vaccinated and a 40-year-old.
Three other measles-related deaths, including two children, were recorded across the United States last year, when the current outbreak began.
The Pennsylvania deaths have prompted a heated debate between the state's Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and President Donald Trump's vaccine-skeptic health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

"This serious situation continues to be made worse by RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety," Shapiro wrote in an X post Tuesday, adding "it's long past time" for Kennedy to "stop stoking vaccine skepticism and misinformation."
Shapiro noted there have been to date 693 recorded cases of measles in Pennsylvania alone. More than 3,290 cases of measles have been recorded across the US since early 2026.

The governor also accused Kennedy of ordering federal officials at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) "to not report these Pennsylvania deaths, presumably because it doesn't fit his narrative."
Kennedy denied that allegation in a response on X, and accused Shapiro of politicizing the "outbreak instead of implementing a unified public health response."
"I have repeatedly stated that MMR vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles," Kennedy said, referring to the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella.
Measles cause fever, respiratory symptoms, skin rashes and can have serious complications, including pneumonia, brain damaging inflammation and death.

The disease was considered eliminated in the US in 2000, thanks to vaccination, but has made a strong comeback in recent years amid declining vaccination rates and a backdrop of growing mistrust of health authorities.
Non-medical exemptions to vaccination have surged since the Covid-19 pandemic, allowing Americans to avoid the shots by invoking religious beliefs or other philosophical reasons.
Before a vaccine was developed in the early 1960s, measles killed hundreds of children every year in the US, and continues to cause tens of thousands of deaths globally.

f6a3148c4270cf25: PETALING JAYA: Seorang pemimpin dari Sabah menegaskan Malaysia tidak memerlukan perjanjian baharu atau ‘new deal’ kerana komitmen dan tanggungjawab dalam Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63) kekal relevan serta mengikat.

Setiausaha Agung Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) Armizan Mohd Ali berkata Artikel VIII MA63 menegaskan komitmen serta tanggungjawab semua pihak yang bersetuju memeterai perjanjian bagi membentuk Persekutuan Malaysia, 63 tahun lalu.

Menurutnya, artikel itu antara lain menetapkan Tanah Melayu (Semenanjung), Borneo Utara (Sabah) dan Sarawak perlu mengambil tindakan perundangan, eksekutif atau tindakan lain yang diperlukan bagi melaksanakan jaminan, komitmen serta syor tertentu dalam Laporan Jawatankuasa Antara Kerajaan (IGC).

Beliau yang juga menteri perdagangan dalam negeri dan kos sara hidup menekankan terma itu penegasan kepada komitmen dan tanggungjawab semua pihak yang bersetuju memeterai perjanjian bagi membentuk Malaysia.
"Melangkah ke hadapan, negara ini tidak memerlukan perjanjian baharu ataupun apa yang disebutkan sebagai ‘new deal’ oleh sesetengah pihak.
"Ini kerana hakikatnya terma-terma perjanjian secara tersurat menzahirkan MA63 itu tidak akan ternoktah sebaik tergubalnya Perlembagaan Persekutuan.
"MA63 itu terus hidup dan komitmen serta tanggungjawab yang digariskan itu kekal relevan dan mengikat dulu, kini dan selamanya," katanya dalam perutusan sempena Hari Malaysia.
Armizan yang juga Ahli Parlimen Papar turut menyeru rakyat memahami nilai dan makna Hari Malaysia dengan lebih mendalam, termasuk menerima kedudukan MA63 dalam sejarah pembentukan negara.
Katanya, pemahaman sejarah negara tidak seharusnya hanya tertumpu kepada Perjanjian Persekutuan Tanah Melayu 1948, kontrak sosial antara tiga kaum utama dan kemerdekaan Tanah Melayu pada 1957.

"Malah menuntut penerimaan sepenuhnya terhadap sijil lahir Persekutuan Malaysia itu sendiri, iaitu MA63," ujarnya sambil mengingatkan 16 Sept tidak diangkat sebagai detik nasional selama lebih 40 tahun selepas pembentukan Malaysia, sebelum Hari Malaysia dimasukkan dalam takwim rasmi negara mulai 2010.
Beliau turut berharap sambutan “63/63” tahun ini bukan sekadar mengenai angka, sebaliknya meningkatkan kefahaman dan penerimaan rakyat terhadap setiap episod sejarah pembentukan Malaysia.
“Moga Malaysia lebih utuh dan maju, tanah air yang makmur dan selamat untuk sekalian rakyatnya,” katanya.
6c294109c867092e: SINGAPORE, Sept 16 — A luxury apartment owned by convicted money launderer Zhang Ruijin is among 26 properties linked to Singapore’s 2023 multibillion-dollar money laundering case that will go under the hammer from this week, The Straits Times (ST) reported.

The 1,991 sq ft four-bedroom unit at Wallich Residence, located on the 61st floor, has a guide price of S$6.78 million and features panoramic views towards Sentosa Cove and the future Greater Southern Waterfront, according to ST.

It is part of the first batch of more than 80 properties that will be auctioned as the Singapore Government moves to liquidate assets seized during investigations into the case. Knight Frank, SRI and ETC have been appointed to conduct the auctions on Sept 17 and 23.

According to the report, Singapore Land Authority records show the Wallich Residence unit is owned by Zhang, a Chinese national who was sentenced to 15 months’ jail after pleading guilty to money laundering and forgery charges.

Zhang’s lover, Lin Baoying, also received a 15-month jail sentence after pleading guilty to similar charges. The pair were deported to Cambodia in June 2024 after serving their sentences, ST reported.

Zhang and Lin were among 10 foreigners from Fujian, China, arrested in the probe. They had bought several luxury properties in prime Singapore developments, including Canninghill Piers, South Beach Residences and Gramercy Park.

The 10 suspects were subsequently jailed and ordered to forfeit their cash and assets. Authorities had targeted S$2.1 billion worth of assets linked to 17 suspects, with 15 of them agreeing to surrender assets valued at about S$1.85 billion in November 2024 in exchange for the withdrawal of Interpol notices against them, ST reported.

Another property on the auction block is a 6,727 sq ft four-bedroom penthouse at South Beach Residences owned by Su Yongcan, who fled Singapore before police operations related to the money laundering case began in August 2023, the report said.

Su’s penthouse, designed by architect Norman Foster, has a guide price of S$25.3 million and will be auctioned on Sept 23. It features grey marble flooring, floor-to-ceiling windows and a large balcony overlooking the Esplanade and Marina Bay.

ST reported that four other Wallich Residence units on the 51st, 53rd, 54th and 61st floors are also being auctioned. The units feature expansive entertainment and family spaces, high-end furnishings and appliances and waterfront views, with three being sold with furnishings.

Other properties include six units at Martin Modern, four freehold units at Gramercy Park and two three-bedroom units at Sloane Residences. Guide prices for the Gramercy Park units range from S$3.8 million to S$7.6 million, while the Sloane Residences units are priced at between S$3.6 million and S$3.7 million.

Property analysts cited by ST said the properties could attract ultra-high-net-worth buyers given the limited supply of large luxury homes in Singapore’s prime districts, although some guide prices were slightly above recent transactions for comparable properties.
96b71dcab5b3da9e: PUTRAJAYA: The home ministry is determined to dismantle the operations of syndicates manipulating the foreign worker system and falsifying documents at the source, without any tolerance, said its minister, Saifuddin Nasution Ismail.
Saifuddin said the immigration department was no longer taking a defensive approach, but was instead acting aggressively to cripple the syndicates at their source.

Saifuddin said the firm action was demonstrated through swift and uncompromising enforcement by the immigration department in Ops Serkap on Sept 14, which saw 11 premises in the Jalan Chan Sow Lin commercial area in Kuala Lumpur raided simultaneously.
He said the operation led to the detention of 30 foreign nationals, including 11 suspected masterminds, comprising 10 men and one woman, all from Bangladesh, operating at the premises.
A total of 19 foreign nationals, comprising 16 Bangladeshis, one Myanmar national and two Indonesians, were detained for various immigration offences.

During the operation, 18 laptops, 21 printers and scanners, three mobile phones and 10 Bangladeshi international passports were seized, along with printed copies of fake electronic Temporary Employment Visit Passes (e-PLKS) and fake police reports.

He said the syndicates’ activities not only undermined the immigration administration system but also posed a threat to public safety and created opportunities for illegal entry by foreigners.
ae96e8daf4edec49: KOTA KINABALU, Sept 16 — The Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63) did not cease to exist upon the enactment of the Federal Constitution but remains in force, with the commitments and responsibilities contained therein continuing to be relevant and binding on all parties, said Minister of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali.

He said this was in line with Article VIII of MA63, which, among other provisions, requires the governments of the Federation of Malaya, North Borneo and Sarawak to take the necessary legislative, executive or other measures to implement the guarantees, undertakings and recommendations contained in Chapter 3 and Annexes A and B of the Inter-Governmental Committee (IGC) Report.

“This term reaffirms the commitment and responsibility of all parties that agreed to sign the agreement to form the Federation of Malaysia,” he said in a Facebook post in conjunction with Malaysia Day today.

Armizan said Malaysia, which was formed in 1963, has now reached 63 years, although Sept 16 only became an important date in the official national calendar and was officially celebrated as Malaysia Day from 2010.

He said understanding the history of Malaysia’s formation should not be limited to the Federation of Malaya Agreement 1948, the social contract among the three major ethnic groups or the independence of Malaya in 1957, but must also include full recognition of MA63 as the “birth certificate” of the Federation of Malaysia.

“In conjunction with this 63/63rd anniversary, let us together understand the value and significance of Malaysia Day by embracing the terms of the agreement signed by the nation’s founders, particularly those enshrined in Article VIII of MA63,” he said.

He added that Malaysia did not require a new agreement or what some parties described as a “new deal”, as the provisions of MA63 clearly indicated that the agreement did not expire following the enactment of the Federal Constitution.
“The commitments and responsibilities outlined therein remain relevant and binding — past, present and future,” he said.
Armizan also expressed hope that Malaysia would continue to develop into a stronger and more advanced nation while ensuring prosperity and security for all Malaysians. — Bernama
31de49c34e2c7573: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 16 — Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) has standardised the entry fee for e-hailing vehicles at RM2, inclusive of tax, across Terminal 1 and Terminal 2, effective today.

Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) in a statement here said the revised fee also represents a reduction from the previous charges of RM3 at Terminal 1 and RM2.16 at Terminal 2, providing passengers with a single, consistent rate for e-hailing pick-ups at both terminals.
It said the standardisation is aimed at providing greater consistency and clarity for passengers and e-hailing operators, while supporting a more streamlined pick-up experience across both terminals.

“This reflects improved control of e-hailing operations, with reduced unauthorised activity, unnecessary vehicle circulation and prolonged idling, while maintaining smooth access for genuine passenger pick-ups.

The enhanced e-hailing system also enables stricter monitoring and access control, helping to ensure that only authorised e-hailing vehicles utilise the designated pick-up facilities. — Bernama
23445f74dccbb741: KUALA LUMPUR: Hari Malaysia disambut setiap 16 Sept sejak 2010 untuk memperingati penubuhan persekutuan Malaysia pada 1963 hasil penyatuan Tanah Melayu, Sabah, Sarawak dan Singapura ketika itu.

Ketua Pengarah Arkib Negara, Zaidin Mohd Noor, berkata proses pembentukan Malaysia melalui beberapa peringkat penting, termasuk selepas Perdana Menteri ketika itu, Tunku Abdul Rahman mengemukakan idea berkenaan pada 1961 yang disusuli rundingan, mesyuarat dan penelitian.

"Kita ada dokumen rasmi, iaitu rekod daripada jabatan kerajaan, fail mesyuarat dan laporan jawatankuasa berkaitan. Contoh dokumen bukan rasmi pula seperti terbitan, akhbar dan gambar.
"Kita melihat ini sebagai rekod sahih atau rekod primer berkenaan dengan sejarah negara kita," katanya ketika ditemui FMT.
Antara rekod berkenaan ialah Laporan Suruhanjaya Cobbold 1962, rekod Jawatankuasa Perundingan Perpaduan Malaysia serta bahan berkaitan 20 Perkara Sabah dan 18 Perkara Sarawak.
Turut terpelihara ialah akhbar terbitan September 1963 dengan gambar Tunku menandatangani Watikah Pemasyhuran Malaysia, selain meja yang digunakan ketika menandatangani watikah itu.
Antara dokumen terpenting ialah Watikah Pemasyhuran Malaysia 1963, yang merekodkan secara rasmi pembentukan Malaysia membabitkan Persekutuan Tanah Melayu, Sabah, Sarawak dan Singapura ketika itu.
Singapura berpisah daripada Malaysia dua tahun kemudian.
Zaidin berkata, rekod asal penting bagi memastikan rakyat, khususnya generasi muda memahami sejarah negara berdasarkan sumber berautoriti, bukannya tafsiran tersebar di media sosial semata-mata.

Selain rekod rasmi kerajaan, beliau berkata, Arkib Negara turut mengumpul bahan daripada individu, pertubuhan bukan kerajaan (NGO) dan pihak swasta bagi mendapatkan rekod daripada perspektif masyarakat yang melalui sesuatu peristiwa.
Menerusi usaha mengumpul 'koleksi rakyat', lebih 5,000 bahan diperoleh, termasuk rekod yang merakam sambutan pembentukan Malaysia di peringkat daerah.
Jejak khazanah masyarakat
Usaha menjejaki khazanah dalam simpanan rakyat turut dilakukan Perpustakaan Negara (PNM) menerusi pengumpulan manuskrip Melayu yang mencatatkan pelbagai ilmu dan kehidupan masyarakat terdahulu.

Timbalan Pengarah Kanan Pusat Kebangsaan Manuskrip Melayu, Fatimah Abdul Hai, berkata lebih 5,000 manuskrip Melayu asal kini disimpan di pusat itu, dengan sebahagian besar dibeli daripada pemilik dan pengumpul individu, selain sumbangan.
"Walaupun kira-kira 70% koleksi berkaitan agama, selebihnya merangkumi sejarah, bahasa dan kesusasteraan, ketatanegaraan, perundangan, perubatan tradisional, pelayaran serta ilmu bintang.

"Ada juga catatan mengenai perkara jarang diketahui hari ini, termasuk petua menjinakkan gajah dan ilmu gastronomi berkaitan pemilihan ramuan, penyediaan makanan serta etika tukang masak," katanya sambil menambah sebahagian daripada pelbagai ilmu itu masih relevan untuk dikaji hari ini.
Setakat ini, kira-kira 2,000 judul manuskrip Melayu telah didigitalkan menerusi MyRepository, dengan akses penuh disediakan kepada pengguna di premis PNM.
Arkib Negara turut mendigitalkan koleksinya, dengan lebih 11 juta bahan melalui proses itu bagi memudahkan rujukan serta mengurangkan pengendalian rekod asal.

Bagi Zaidin, usaha memelihara rekod hari ini bukan sahaja penting untuk memahami perjalanan membawa kepada pembentukan Malaysia, tetapi juga menentukan apa yang dapat diketahui generasi akan datang mengenai sejarah negara.

f866c3f572b1ef88: TypeSafe AI, a startup bestowed with $40 million in funding, on Tuesday declared itself a maker of frontier models with the release of Jev, a new type of AI model intended for interaction with machines rather than people. Instead of returning natural language in response to a text-based prompt, TypeSafe AI designed Jev to return typed probabilistic decisions for use by other software or AI models. Type safety in programming is a way to catch errors that arise when software processes an unexpected type of data, as might happen if an operation tried to divide an integer by a text string. By providing typed, structured values, Jev can avoid the parsing and validating that must be done to process text responses from LLMs. This approach can be useful for scenarios where interactions with an AI system need to be constrained to a limited set of answers. It can, for example, play Doom, when fed structured data describing the player's game state. But it's more likely to be used for sorting customer service problems and other business workflows. With Jev, the developer starts with a state value, which can be a JSON object or simply a string like "My card was charged twice." The model gets presented with state information through a set of question primitives (Choice, Score, Noul), each of which returns a different type of structured response with probabilities. So a question asking the model to choose which of three departments should handle a particular customer service query might come back: {"billing": 0.08, "technical": 0.85, "sales": 0.07}, with a confidence score of 0.82. That's not very useful for a person seeking the answer to a question but for a software developer, that might be just the thing to make a particular customer service function run more reliably. Jev is a System One model, which relies on a different architecture called Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, is a former OpenAI researcher and one of the co-inventors of reinforcement learning for human feedback (RLHF) and ChatGPT. "TypeSafe was founded to pursue an alternative path for AI research, focused on machine-native AI," said Almeida in a statement. "I spent years working on models designed to make AI better at interacting with people. But if AI is going to fundamentally change how work gets done, people can't be the only consumers of intelligence." While natural language responses from the likes of ChatGPT or Claude can be wrapped in other code to produce a constrained set of responses, Jev's appeal follows from its efficiency. TypeSafe claims that LLMs generally have variable response times that can stretch into minutes. Jev's response time supposedly ranges from 70ms-500ms, 40x-200x faster than traditional LLMs. The model achieves this speed by using parallel processing. LLMs like OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Terra predict the next text token in a sequence and thus operate sequentially. The System One architecture returns all outputs to a query at once. The demo posted on the TypeSafe website shows Jev returning a response in 0.114s, compared to 8.566 seconds for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Terra. Then there's the issue of cost. Jev charges $0.042 / MTok for input and $0 for output. OpenAI GPT-5.6 Terra costs $2.00 / MTok and $12 / MTok for output. And compared to a top tier model like Fable 5.1, Jev costs 238x less. The name "Jev" is a reference to 19th century English economist William Stanley Jevons, known for Jevons paradox, who argued that technology efficiency related to coal usage increased coal consumption rather than reducing it. The name also reflects the AI industry's bet that greater token efficiency will increase token consumption even as token prices decline. That wager assumes the market for tokens will be as broad as the market for energy – an assumption that isn't yet settled given that many people who have access to AI tools just don't have a use for them or avoid AI tools due to moral objections. TypeSafe claims that Jev is hallucination-free, which really isn't a fair comparison as its output is not natural language. Jev instead returns structured responses with probabilities, and that does not preclude the possibility of being incorrect. TypeSafe's model won't be the source of misinformation like fabricated legal citations but it also won't be used in the same way since its responses are intended to be consumed by software. Where this becomes relevant is when handling AI agent tool calls and automation. "Having a hallucinated tool call is inconvenient in an agent, but is an absolute deal-breaker if it’s part of a system with latency guarantees or it’s buried several layers deep in a dependency chain," the company claims in its blog post. "Existing models, no matter how smart, still hallucinate and have type errors." Jev, TypeSafe claims, is well-suited for AI automation software, real-time applications that need quick decisions, AI map reduce jobs for classifying large corpora of data, verification of AI inputs, and AI model harnesses. And if it can play Doom as well and as efficiently as advertised, it may not be long before users ask Jev to make drone targeting decisions. ®

1ae9beea168ea7a3: Kita perlu jujur mengakui ramai di antara kita tidaklah terlalu excited pasal Hari Malaysia. 'Kita' disini merujuk warga Malaysia orang Semenanjung.
Mujur ada acara 'Keretapi Sarong' disamping beberapa aktiviti kebudayaan. Ada juga kemeriahan.

Tetapi itu di Kuala Lumpur. Di tempat lain agak sepi kerana upacara sambutan sudah dibuat pada 31 Ogos. Kita lebih 'feel' 31 Ogos. Our brothers and sisters di Borneo pula tidak excited pada 31 Ogos sebab kata mereka itu tarikh Malaya merdeka.
Yang besar buat mereka ialah Hari Malaysia .
Kata mereka Malaya sudah tidak wujud sejak Malaysia ditubuhkan pada 1963. Maka yang mesti diraikan Hari Malaysia– 16 Sept. They have a point. Valid.
Tetapi di Semenanjung, rakyat Malaysia tetap mengaitkan 31 Ogos dengan kemerdekaan negara merujuk Ogos 1957. Masih melaung 'Merdeka' setiap tahun apabila datangnya 31 Ogos.
Meskipun kerajaan telah sekian lama menetapkan 31 Ogos sebagai Hari Kebangsaan. Bukan Hari Kemerdekaan.
Pada 31 Ogos baru-baru ini ramai yang menganggapnya hari ulang tahun Malaysia merdeka kali ke-69 jelas mengambil kira 1957. Tahun depan sambutan pasti grand kerana hari kemerdekaan ke-70 kata mereka.

Tidak boleh dipersalahkan mereka berpandangan begitu. Malah di sekolah anak-anak diajar 31 Ogos ialah hari Malaysia merdeka. Jika mereka (termasuk anak-anak Sabah dan Sarawak) beri jawapan lain daripada tarikh itu semasa mengambil ujian sejarah tanah air misalnya, mereka tidak akan dapat markah.
Pada hal, saya ulangi 31 Ogos 1957 Malaya yang merdeka. Dan untuk mengatakan Malaysia merdeka juga tidak betul. Malaysia hanya wujud pada 16 Sept 1963. Ia ditubuhkan. Ia tidak merdeka.
Daripada siapa pula ia memerdekakan diri?

Penubuhan Malaysia ialah apabila Sabah, Sarawak juga Singapura bergabung dengan Malaya. Sehingga sekarang saudara kita di Sabah dan Sarawak cukup tidak senang (sebenarnya marah) apabila kita kata Sabah dan Sarawak 'masuk Malaysia'.

Mereka tidak 'masuk' mana-mana negara– apa lagi 'masuk' sesuatu yang belum wujud pun waktu itu. Diulangi mereka bergabung dengan Malaya untuk menubuhkan Malaysia. Oleh itu 16 Sept ialah hari kelahiran Malaysia.
Hatta ucapan paling tepat pada hari itu ialah Selamat Hari Lahir Malaysia.
Sudah tiba masa pihak berwajib memperbetulkan fakta sejarah negara. Once and for all.
Pada beberapa penulisan sebelum ini saya pernah menyarankan 31 Ogos hanya cuti umum buat Semenanjung. Ucapannya pula ialah Selamat merdeka Semenanjung Malaysia. Istilah Hari Kebangsaan dilesapkan.
Upacara sambutan diadakan secara sederhana.

Di Sabah cuti umum diisytiharkan juga 31 Ogos iaitu tarikh ia mendapat status memerintah atau self rule daripada Inggeris pada 1963. Di Sarawak beri cuti umum untuk 22 Julai iaitu tarikh self rule mereka juga diperolehi pada 1963.
Ertinya saya sarankan Semenanjung, Sabah dan Sarawak sambut hari merdeka masing-masing pada tarikh yang disebut tadi.
Namun pada 16 Sept iaitu Hari Malaysia disambut gilang gemilang diraikan di Semenanjung, Sabah dan Sarawak bersama-sama sebagai satu rakyat Malaysia. Lantas tajuk artikel ini.
Itu sekadar cadangan saya yang tidak dihiraukan. Come to think of it tiada siapa pun yang minta saya utarakan cadangan in the first place. Saya sahaja yang 'syok sendiri'.
Apa pun teringat satu laporan akhbar The Sun Daily pada Sept 2013 mengenai salah seorang pengasas penubuhan Malaysia dari Sarawak bernama Dominic Andrew Dagok anak Randen.

Menurut beliau oleh kerana waktu itu Brunei dikatakan berminat bergabung dengan Malaya, Sabah (yang dikenali sebagai North Borneo), Sarawak dan Singapura, parti beliau yang dikenali sebagia 'Panas' mencadangkan negara atau persekutuan yang akan ditubuhkan diberi nama 'Borbrusima'.
'Borbrusima' ialah singkatan untuk Borneo, Brunei, Singapura dan Malaya”. Ini kata Dominic Andrew Dagok ialah untuk memberi gambar tepat akan komposisi negara yang bakal ditubuhkan.
Bagaimanapun ramai pemimpin tidak setuju.
Bayangkan jika Brobrusima dipilih sebagai nama negara ini. Apa agaknya nama baru yang akan digunakan apabila Singapura keluar meninggalkan persekutuan pada 8 Ogos 1965?
Mujurlah nama sedap didengar dipilih sebagai nama negara ini. Buat Malaysia – Selamat Hari Malaysia.

b7278884c8957dfd: Many things could be done better in Malaysia, but I don’t have the energy, skill or fortitude to do them myself. Therefore, I choose to be more forgiving to those with good hearts who dive into the cesspool of politics to try to make things better.

Only those with good hearts, mind you! People who make tough choices and compromises and sacrifices but whose moral compass remains true. There aren’t many of those, so I’m not overly strained with having to accommodate them.

Recently I read some cautious statements that perhaps the affirmative action programmes which are the backbone of our national politics should be amended or phased out. However, these voices are mostly on the periphery of national politics.

Their positions are often couched in careful terms - perhaps a phased withdrawal at some uncertain date in the future or perhaps some amendments to the current programmes. Some convolute things by arguing for both “meritocracy” as well as some form of continuing affirmative action as the Malays aren’t quite ready to cut the ties to those affirmative actions yet.
False meritocracy

I’m generally not a big fan of this “meritocracy” argument. It’s often just people arguing for their own privileges, whether wealth, culture or some other forms of advantages that cement their head start, while simplistically conflating meritocracy purely through exam results and grades.

I’d rather affirmative actions be directed towards those who really need them, regardless of background. I’m myself a beneficiary of earlier affirmative actions, without which I’d probably just be a poor fisherman off Bayan Lepas staring at unemployment as the sea itself is swallowed up by artificial islands.

The original set of affirmative actions – the New Economic Policy – were actually meant to expire in 1990. That it did not wasn’t a big surprise. In 1990 many Malays were still living in remote villages far away from electricity, schools or hospitals. The aim of changing centuries of neglect within just a generation was too optimistic.

You can easily send young Malays for university education, but success in today’s capitalistic world requires a total mindset change. That transformation is difficult and carries the dangers of killing what is good about Malays – the gentle, warm and friendly folks not quite made for the dog-eat-dog world around us.
Casualties of NEP
The resulting inflamed racial politics benefited some people inordinately at the expense of the many, both Malays and non-Malays.

Another casualty is that the Malays of old, the incorruptible ones – the likes of Onn Jaafar, Dr Ismail Abdul Rahman and Ismail Ali – are mostly gone and no amount of increased piety and religiosity can replace them.

The dominant Malay mindset is one of entitlement. Behind this, however, lies something sadder: insecurity. The same insecurity made us meekly submit to four and a half centuries of colonisation and to our own feudal lords and others where fealty, often unearned, to our “betters” is expected.

Affirmative actions have helped, but also have hurt us. The crutches that helped us stand higher in the economic and other struggles unfortunately have become permanent, which we dare not contemplate living without.
Shackles of fear

Much of the claims of rights and privileges for being the original “sons of the soil” amount to just political manipulation; but they work, because of the fear among many Malays of flying untethered and competing on the same level playing fields as others.

This fear, this insecurity, hurts us. they have become institutionalised and encoded into our psyche. Privileges became rights, the temporary became permanent, regardless of what the Constitution and common sense say.

We invent new logic to support our argument. The latest came from a bunch of political ladies (some who may appear to be "constitutional" rather than ethnic Malays) who say that the old New Economic Policy goal of Malays owning 30% of the corporate wealth should now be raised to 50%, presumably as being a fairer reflection of today’s demographics.
If so, then past exhortations for Malays to reproduce aggressively so that we can “protect” the race have actually proven useful for some.
Greedy elites

Had this been an aspirational goal driving an agenda of advancement (you know, the boring stuff like smaller families, better education, stronger pride of “berdikari” – standing on our own two feet) I’d be the first to applaud it. However, this is just a pretext to carve out even more of the nation’s wealth that we couldn’t earn on our own.

This really is just about a bunch of Malay elites salivating about using politics to gain and protect easy wealth for themselves, which may result in the creation of unit trust funds meant for the bumiputera masses.

Should this happen, what will come to pass is of even more corporate wealth being owned and run by cronies and GLCs and shadowy and corrupt enablers. We’ll have even more Malay billionaires – official ones anyway – but we’ll also have more Malay families struggling to make ends meet.

We’ll never reach 50% because who wants to kill the goose that lays the golden egg? The number of Malays who struggle daily to put food on the table of their large families will remain high because they’re a convenient excuse for politicians.

More non-Malays will feel disenfranchised. Many Malays – those who have options elsewhere – will also be disheartened. Then one day we may even demand 100% of the corporate pie for Malays because Malaysia has lost all non-Malays even while the economic pie itself has shrunk to a measly cookie.
Take off the crutches

When we celebrate national independence -- which no West Malaysian alive (except for perhaps one) had actually fought for -- we talk about being independent of colonisers, we don’t talk enough about being independent in our own mind. We’re still haunted by fears of others not like us and easily kept in line by our own who are supposedly “better” than us.
And so here we are, not just politically independent but a nation that’s an even more complex and volatile mix.

It's about time we accept that not everything is about us and that we’re actually tougher than we think – if only we dare to put ourselves to the test. Enough with this rubbish about extending affirmative action. They helped to make us stronger, but now they are making us weaker. We’re now more addicted, more frightened and more angry when we think about living without the privileges.

Let’s have a different kind of conversation. Let’s accept that true independence is being able to stand on our two feet and being able to help others instead of asking help for ourselves. For Malaysia to succeed, we Malays must feel confident we can happily and independently co-exist with fellow Malaysians without worrying about our survival.
With that, Happy Malaysia Day to one and all Malaysians.

95111bbc82fce2a5: Malaysian football has seen plenty of new beginnings.
This one comes with a particularly familiar cast.

The Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) goes to the polls tomorrow to elect a president and a new executive committee, seven months after its entire 17-member leadership stepped down following an AFC governance review.
The statutes have been rewritten, the executive committee cut to 11 members, clubs given a greater formal voice and eligibility rules tightened.
On paper, the machinery looks different.
Then comes the candidate list.

Of the 28 candidates whose eligibility and intention to contest have been confirmed, 17 have established FAM connections, including 12 who served on the executive committee that resigned en masse in January.
Only 11 are newcomers who have never sat on FAM’s executive board.
That sits uneasily with an election being presented as the start of a new era.
So why should anyone believe FAM will really change when so much of the old FAM is still seeking a seat at the table?
FAM’s credibility was damaged by a governance failure. Its response was to replace the leadership, submit to an external review and rewrite the rules.
Now a significant proportion of the people from that previous administration are seeking office again.
So what, precisely, is the election supposed to demonstrate?
The answer cannot simply be that the rules have changed.
Rules matter, but rules do not govern football. People do.
That makes this election more than a contest between Ab Ghani Hassan and Shahril Mokhtar for the presidency.
Both come with administrative credentials. Ghani heads the Malaysian Football League, while Shahril is deputy president of the Football Association of Selangor.
Their supporters can make the case for their experience, programmes and ability to lead.
But whoever wins inherits a problem much larger than the presidency.
FAM needs credibility.
That became painfully clear last year when Fifa sanctioned FAM over falsified documentation used in the registration of seven foreign-born players.
Fifa fined the association about RM1.9 million and banned the players for 12 months. The Court of Arbitration for Sport later upheld the disciplinary consequences.
The finding went beyond an administrative lapse. Fifa said using fraudulent documentation to make a player eligible to compete amounted to cheating and damaged trust in the fairness of football.
That trust is now central to Malaysian football’s recovery.
Changing the furniture will not restore it.

The January mass resignation was supposed to mark a decisive break. FAM said the executive committee’s departure would protect the association’s integrity and reputation, allow investigations and internal processes to proceed without interference, and help restore public confidence.
Those were serious words.
Seven months later, some of the same people are seeking office again.
There is nothing inherently improper about an experienced administrator standing for election.
Previous service should not become a lifetime ban from public office. Nor should every former office-bearer carry personal responsibility for every failure during a collective tenure.
But an organisation emerging from a governance crisis cannot expect the public to ignore the symbolism.
If the mass resignation was part of the process of rebuilding confidence, what does it say when much of the same political ecosystem reappears at the next election?
This is not about personalities but about institutional memory.
For months, FAM has responded to pressure from outside, first with Fifa sanctions, then an AFC governance review and finally a rewrite of its statutes shaped by the continental body.
Now the association has to show that it can govern differently without waiting for another crisis, another audit or another international intervention to tell it what needs fixing.

The new statutes give FAM useful tools. A smaller executive committee should make responsibility clearer. Greater representation for professional clubs could broaden decision-making. Tighter eligibility rules should raise the standard for those seeking office.
But no statute can guarantee good governance.
A carefully rewritten rulebook can still sit in the hands of people comfortable with old habits.
That is why the composition of the new executive committee matters as much as the identity of the president.

Will members challenge decisions when they should? Will they insist on proper documentation? Will they accept scrutiny? Will they put the association’s interests ahead of personal, state or club loyalties?
And will anyone tell a powerful colleague when something is wrong?
The public, meanwhile, is not obliged to regard Sept 17 as a cure.
For many supporters, this will be another event inside a football administration that has spent too long asking for patience.

The national team continues to deal with the fallout from the naturalisation scandal, Fifa’s sanctions remain in force and Malaysian football is still trying to repair a reputation damaged far beyond its own borders.
A new president cannot erase that with a victory speech.
Nor can a new executive committee demand confidence simply because affiliates have elected it.
Confidence will return only when FAM makes decisions that withstand scrutiny and accepts accountability when things go wrong.
That means looking beyond the campaign.
The real measure will be whether the new leadership strengthens internal controls, demands proper governance and gives newcomers room to challenge established thinking.
It will also be whether returning administrators recognise that experience has value only when it comes with the willingness to confront what went wrong.
An election can change who occupies the room without changing what happens inside it. That is why the return of so many familiar figures deserves scrutiny.

After everything Malaysian football has been through, FAM is asking the public to believe that a new structure will deliver a different culture while many of the people from the old structure are asking for another turn at running it.
The question is no longer whether FAM can announce a new beginning. It is whether anyone outside the room has enough reason to believe it.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
